title: Case study: Building a portfolio for a family
subtitle: Family portfolio example
openingQuestion: Nam (38) and Hanh (36) have 2 children (5 and 8), combined income of 45 million VND/month, a 6-month emergency fund already built, and no bad debt (only a mortgage with a good rate left). Goals: a college education fund for the 2 children (10-13 years away) and retirement (22 years away). What's a sensible priority order for allocating their monthly savings?
openingOptions: Only invest 100% of monthly savings in stocks, since both spouses are still young and don't need to worry at all about this money's safety
Put 100% of monthly savings into the children's education fund since that's the nearer goal, ignoring retirement entirely because it seems far off
Keep the emergency fund and insurance, then split savings between both retirement and education
No financial allocation plan is needed at all - just leave all leftover money each month in a checking account
explanation: With several financial goals happening at once (children's education in the near/medium term, retirement in the long term), the principle is to not pour all resources into one goal while neglecting another - especially retirement, since a longer accumulation horizon means starting early captures a big compounding advantage, while delaying it requires a much higher catch-up contribution later. At the same time, the children's education fund (10-13 years) should have a rising share of safe assets as its deadline approaches, unlike the retirement portfolio (22 years), which can maintain a higher growth weighting in its early stage.

diagram.label: Allocate resources separately for each goal

realWorldExample.company: A composite case: a two-child family in Hanoi/Ho Chi Minh City
realWorldExample.description: This is a case study illustrating how to apply the concepts covered throughout this track (emergency fund, insurance, goal-based asset allocation, portfolio rebalancing) to a specific family situation - not a real company or financial product, but a composite exercise letting learners see the full picture of personal/family financial planning.

quiz.question: Why should Nam's family NOT put 100% of their savings into the children's education fund while ignoring retirement, even though education seems more 'urgent'?
options: Because the state will cover most university tuition
Because an education fund set up for children always earns a lower return than a retirement fund does
Because the law doesn't allow withdrawing a pension fund to pay tuition
Because retirement has a longer accumulation horizon, and children can borrow
quiz.explanation: A common principle in family financial planning: don't fully sacrifice retirement for children's education, since there are several ways to fund education (scholarships, student loans) but no 'retirement loan' can make up for a shortfall in savings in old age.

quiz.question: Why should the children's education fund (10-13 years) gradually lower its high-risk asset weighting (stocks) as its deadline approaches, while the retirement fund (22 years) can keep a higher growth weighting in its early stage?
options: Because the closer you get to needing the money, the less time there is to recover
Because stocks always fall sharply in the final years of a cycle
Because money set aside for children must always be kept much safer than money set aside for retirement
Because education funds are legally capped in how much stock they can hold
quiz.explanation: The time-horizon allocation principle: the closer a goal, the more volatility needs to be reduced to avoid the risk of having to sell assets right when the market is down, with no time left to wait for recovery.

quiz.question: A family has two goals: tuition for a child in 5 years and retirement in 25 years. What should they do?
options: Combine them into one single portfolio at an averaged risk level
Split them into two separate portfolios with different risk levels by horizon
Pour everything into the nearer goal first, then worry about the far one
Keep everything sitting in a bank deposit until each goal's deadline arrives, then figure out what to do
quiz.explanation: Money needed in 5 years shouldn't sit in the same place as money needed in 25 years - a 30% drop in year four would wreck the tuition goal while having no impact on retirement at all.

quiz.question: Where should the emergency fund rank in a family's order of priority?
options: Simultaneously with investing, splitting the family's monthly savings evenly in half between the two
Only after the long-term investment portfolio has already been fully built out for both spouses
Before any investment at all, since it prevents having to sell assets in a bad market
Not necessary at all, as long as the family already carries health insurance and life insurance
quiz.explanation: Without an emergency fund, an incident forces you to sell the portfolio right when it's down - turning a temporary loss into a permanent one. This is why it comes before even the very first investment.

quiz.question: A couple has very different risk tolerances. How should this be handled sensibly?
options: Pick the mathematical average of the two spouses' tolerances and keep that fixed for the rest of their lives
Split the household assets exactly in half, letting each spouse invest purely according to their own personal tolerance
Simply follow the risk tolerance of whichever spouse happens to earn the higher income
Pick a risk level the more cautious spouse can still sleep with, then revisit periodically
quiz.explanation: A portfolio that keeps one person up at night gets sold at the bottom - and the seller doesn't care what averaging method set the weighting. The starting point is a level both can tolerate, then adjust gradually.

quiz.question: Where should insurance sit in the financial plan of a family with young children?
options: Right after the emergency fund, before expanding the long-term investment portfolio
Last, only bought once the investment portfolio has already hit its original target
Unnecessary if the family already has a six-month emergency fund
Even before the emergency fund, since insurance matters more than a cash buffer
quiz.explanation: The emergency fund covers small shocks; insurance covers shocks that can wipe out the entire plan. For a family with dependent children, a gap in insurance is a far bigger risk than investing a few months late.

keyTakeaways: With several financial goals at once, allocate resources sensibly across each - don't pour everything into one and neglect another, especially retirement
Each financial goal should have its own portfolio suited to its own time horizon - the closer the goal, the higher the safe-asset weighting
A basic emergency fund and protective insurance are the foundation needed before optimizing other long-term investment goals
This case study is a composite of the concepts covered in this track - try applying the same approach to your own real financial situation

practicePrompt.question: Nam's family is torn between putting all 15 million/month of savings into the 2 children's education fund (10-13 years away) first, then starting retirement savings only once the children start college. Is this a sensible order of priority?
options: Not sensible - they should split savings between both goals in parallel right away, since retirement has 22 years for compounding to work
Sensible, since children's education is always more important than retirement and should be prioritized ahead of any other goal
Sensible, since retirement is still 22 years away, so it's entirely fine to start saving for it later with no effect on the final result
The order doesn't matter, since children can always borrow for tuition and aging parents can similarly borrow to retire
practicePrompt.explanation: Resources should be split between both goals in parallel - delaying retirement to prioritize children's education would require a much higher catch-up contribution later, while children can borrow for tuition but aging parents can't 'borrow' to retire.

summary.keyIdea: With several financial goals at once, allocate resources sensibly across each - don't pour everything into one and neglect another, especially retirement
summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a phrase to memorize rather than a principle to apply to a real decision.

application.title: Try applying it
application.message: If you have several financial goals (buying a home, tuition, retirement), write down the time horizon for each and estimate the safe/growth weighting each one should have.
application.secondary: It doesn't need to be perfect right away - just start separating each goal out.

sections.text: Financial knowledge only really has value once applied to a specific situation. This case study pulls together the concepts covered throughout this track - emergency fund, insurance, goal-based asset allocation - into a real family problem.

Nam and Hanh's family is a typical example of many middle-class urban families in Vietnam: stable income, a basic safety foundation already built (emergency fund, no bad debt), but facing several financial goals at once that need sensible balancing, rather than focusing on just one.
Step 1 - Confirm the safety foundation is solid

Before allocating money to any investment goal, two foundations need to be secure: an emergency fund (the family already has 6 months of expenses - meeting the standard) and adequate protective insurance (Nam, as the main breadwinner, needs sufficient term life insurance, and both spouses should have health insurance). This step can't be skipped, because without this foundation, an unexpected event (job loss, illness) could wreck the entire long-term plan behind it.
Step 2 - Allocate across two goals with different time horizons

items: Children's education fund (10-13 years): early on, can allocate moderate growth (60-70% stocks/diversified funds, 30-40% bonds/deposits), gradually lowering the risk weighting as the children approach college (2-3 years left) to preserve capital
Retirement fund (22 years): with much more time, can maintain a higher growth weighting (70-80% stocks/diversified funds) in its early stage, lowering it as retirement age approaches
Don't pour 100% into one goal - set a fixed monthly contribution rate for both funds in parallel, adjusted to the family's actual cash flow
Take advantage of compounding: starting retirement contributions early, even in small amounts, beats piling everything into a later stage

sections.label: A simple illustrative figure
sections.text: Suppose the family sets aside 10 million VND/month for both goals: they could allocate 6 million/month to the retirement fund (long-term investing, higher growth weighting) and 4 million/month to the children's education fund (shorter horizon, rising safe-asset weighting). The specific split should be adjusted to each family's priorities and risk tolerance - there's no single rigid formula.

lines: There's no 'standard' portfolio that applies to every family - what matters is clearly identifying each goal, its corresponding time horizon, and allocating assets suited to that goal.

Try applying the same approach to your own financial situation: list your goals, determine each one's time horizon, and allocate resources in a balanced way instead of pouring everything in one direction.
